Eggs of the Chestnut teal (Anas castanea) are deposited in nests lined with down and concealed in dense vegetation near brackish wetlands. Field studies have recorded that females lay a clutch of 7 to 10 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 7 to 10 eggs per nesting attempt], and available data indicate that only a single clutch is produced annually [F_R_i = single clutch is produced annually]. The incubation period progresses at a steady temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], with the eggs hatching after approximately 26 days [ab = approximately 26 days], a duration that aligns with that of other dabbling ducks of comparable egg size. Newly emerged ducklings are precocial and weigh about 34 grams [Wwb = about 34 grams] at birth, a relatively modest mass that nonetheless endows them with sufficient yolk reserves to sustain initial activity before their first forays into exogenous feeding. This hatching mass is notably lower than the initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg, which is recorded at 40 grams [Ww0 = 40 grams], reflecting the metabolic consumption and water loss that occur during the roughly four-week incubation period under natural conditions.

The developmental trajectory from hatching to fledging in Chestnut teal unfolds at the species' typical active body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, the time elapsed between hatching and the achievement of sustained flight is 34 days [tx = 34 days], a period during which the downy chick transforms into a fully feathered juvenile capable of independent locomotion at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This fledging age represents a critical milestone, as it marks the transition from complete dependence on parental care to a stage where the young bird can begin to forage alongside the hen in shallow estuarine waters. Following fledging, the juveniles enter a prolonged phase of somatic growth and social integration, gradually acquiring the skills necessary for survival. The onset of gonadal maturation, or puberty, is reached considerably later than the achievement of flight. Specifically, field observations indicate that individuals attain puberty at 102 days after hatching [tp = 102 days after hatching], a delay that reflects the substantial energetic investment required to complete the development of the reproductive system in a species that inhabits seasonally variable coastal environments at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].

Sexual size dimorphism is pronounced in Chestnut teal, with males ultimately attaining a larger asymptotic body mass than females. The ultimate wet weight for males has been documented at 671.5 grams [Wwi = 671.5 grams], whereas the corresponding value for females is 591.5 grams [Wwi = 591.5 grams]. This difference of roughly 80 grams is consistent with the typical pattern observed in many Anatidae, where males are heavier-bodied, likely due to the selective pressures associated with mate competition and territory defense during the breeding season. These adult masses represent a substantial increase over the neonatal body mass of 34 grams, indicating a growth multiple of approximately 17- to 20-fold from hatching to adulthood. The disparity in ultimate size also has implications for the metabolic requirements of each sex, as larger individuals generally incur higher daily energetic costs. The reported values for maximum adult mass are derived from measurements of wild-caught individuals during the non-breeding season, thus reflecting the condition of birds not burdened by the additional energetic loads of reproduction or molt.

Basal metabolic rate has been quantified in Chestnut teal through respirometry trials conducted under controlled thermal conditions. At a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the maximum basal oxygen consumption recorded is 343 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 343 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic rate, when considered in the context of the species' ultimate wet weight for males of 671.5 grams, yields a mass-specific value that is broadly consistent with the allometric predictions for a waterfowl of this size. The measurement was obtained from post-absorptive, resting birds during the thermoneutral zone, ensuring that the value represents genuine basal metabolism rather than the elevated rates associated with digestion, locomotion, or thermoregulation. Interestingly, this metabolic rate is recorded under the same thermal conditions as several other key life-history parameters—including fledging age, puberty, and lifespan—suggesting that the species operates within a relatively narrow thermal window for its physiological activities. The ability to maintain this body temperature is likely facilitated by the dense plumage and the capacity to shunt blood flow to the unfeathered legs, a common thermoregulatory adaptation among waterfowl that allows for heat dissipation without compromising core temperature.

This extended lifespan is achieved at the species' characteristic active body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The timing of this first brood is closely tied to the seasonal availability of invertebrate prey in coastal wetlands, which peaks during the austral spring. Given the clutch size of 7 to 10 eggs produced in a single annual nesting attempt, the lifetime reproductive output of a female that survives to senescence can be considerable, though it is subject to substantial variation driven by environmental stochasticity and predation pressure on nests. The interplay between a long reproductive lifespan and a modest annual fecundity underscores a life-history strategy oriented toward adult survival rather than high immediate reproductive returns.
